reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes purchasing cloud-mining pools with promised payouts and specific mining-share prices and terms. It provides a participation and payment walkthrough involving a $99 enrollment fee and cryptocurrency transfer to a displayed Bitcoin Cash invoice within a 10-minute window. the available video evidence does not establish whether the service operated, payouts were made, or viewers experienced losses.

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker gives viewers cautions that matter before they act. He warns, “Don't send Bitcoin to Bitcoin Cash address. It won't work,” and tells them to confirm both the address and amount before sending. He also says the mining contract will not start for the first thirty days. These are operational warnings and a disclosed delay, not a guarantee that a viewer will profit. The recording explains a transaction while leaving its eventual financial result unproven.

citations.quote: Don't send Bitcoin to Bitcoin Cash address. It won't work.

Please note it will not start for the first thirty days.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited daily-payout line describes what the dashboard's clock indicates; it does not demonstrate that a payout occurred or promise a fixed amount to this viewer. The 1000-day term describes a contract's duration, while the speaker separately discloses that it will not start immediately. The enrollment fee is expressly tied to activating an account, not presented as a fee that unlocks guaranteed earnings.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Warnings about sending the correct currency and the delayed start do not change the core offer. The speaker directs viewers through purchasing a mining pool and paying for it, while describing payouts every 24 hours based on the pool held. A disclosed delay is still part of a paid-mining returns pitch; the question does not require proof that anyone received a payout or suffered a loss.

opening.argument: Judge, the video's stated purpose is account setup, and its scope includes registration, login, purchasing, payment, and an exchange. The speaker uses his own account to demonstrate an order and says he will discuss the pros and cons of repurchase settings in another video. That makes this a walkthrough of how an interface works. Showing a purchase path, even one involving mining, does not by itself establish that the speaker verified the service's payouts or guaranteed an investment outcome.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing opening accurately identifies a purchase walkthrough, but a walkthrough is the very subject announced in the title. Its payout quotation describes the dashboard's schedule, not a demonstrated payment to a participant. The $99 enrollment mention establishes a stated account cost, not that this speaker has proved any eventual return. Those distinctions matter when interpreting a tutorial as an endorsement of an unverified outcome.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The tutorial framing does not make this merely an abstract technology lesson. The speaker offers a link, explains how to buy a pool, and walks through sending Bitcoin Cash to pay for it. He connects that purchase to a stated daily payout schedule. His own purchase demonstration supports, rather than distances him from, the paid-mining offer.

opening.argument: Judge, the transaction is presented as buying a specified mining-pool contract through a shop, with a stated 1000-day term. The speaker separately identifies a one-time enrollment charge and describes paying the pool invoice in Bitcoin Cash. That is evidence of a priced service and a payment process, but not evidence here of a guaranteed rate of return, a required recruitment payment, or a realized loss. The daily payout description is conditional on which pool someone holds, not a quoted profit figure.

rebuttal.rebuttal: A payment address and a 10-minute invoice window show how this particular purchase is processed; neither establishes what happened after payment. The cited enrollment fee is described as activating the account, while the 1000-day figure is the stated length of the purchased mining contract. The opposing opening rightly notes that actual operation and losses are unestablished. The evidence therefore supports a purchase demonstration more directly than a claim about a proven fraudulent outcome.
